name: Vanuatu
summary: A Y-shaped chain of about 80 islands, once the New Hebrides, run jointly by Britain and France (1906–80) before independence in 1980.

knownFor.label: Land diving
knownFor.note: Pentecost Island jumps that inspired bungee jumping.

location.value: South Pacific archipelago; the infobox gives 12,189 km² and the text about 12,274 km²; capital and largest city Port Vila on Efate.

terrain.value: Volcanic and coral islands with rugged mountains and active volcanoes such as Yasur on Tanna and Ambrym; Espiritu Santo is the largest island.

climate.value: Tropical, hot and humid, with a wet cyclone season from November to April; cooler in the southern islands.

resources.value: Fertile volcanic soil for copra, kava, cocoa and beef cattle, plus fish, and beaches and reefs that attract tourists.

disasters.value: Cyclone Pam struck in March 2015 as a Category 5 cyclone; the page gives 11 deaths early on and 16 deaths later.

population.value: 300,019 at the 2020 census; 335,908 in the 2023 estimate.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; about a quarter live in towns, chiefly Port Vila on Efate and Luganville on Espiritu Santo.

disease.value: Diabetes and heart disease from imported food.

migration.value: Many work seasonally on farms in Australia and New Zealand; people also move from outer islands to Port Vila.

economicBase.value: Agriculture supports 65% of the population, with copra and kava the main earners; tourist arrivals were 196,134 in 2008; it is a tax haven with no income tax; citizenship sales (about $150,000) may exceed 30% of revenue.

tradeRoutes.value: Ports at Port Vila and Luganville and airports with links to Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and New Caledonia.

moneyAndTax.value: The vatu, introduced in 1981; there is no income tax, so the state relies on import duties and a value-added tax.

inequality.value: Gap between the capital and outer islands.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary republic (infobox) with a 52-member one-chamber Parliament.

keyRulers.value: Walter Lini led Vanuatu to independence on 30 July 1980 as first prime minister and served until 1991.

succession.value: Prime ministers change through elections and through frequent votes of no confidence in Parliament.

institutions.value: A single-chamber Parliament, a president, courts, and the Malvatumauri (National Council of Chiefs), which advises on custom.

stability.value: Coconut War (1980); frequent changes of government.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between English-speaking (Anglophone) and French-speaking (Francophone) parties, and later frequent coalition changes.

armyAndTech.value: No army; the Vanuatu Police Force includes a paramilitary wing, the Vanuatu Mobile Force.

majorWars.value: In 1980 Espiritu Santo seceded as the Republic of Vemarana, followed by a brief conflict the page calls the Coconut War.

territoryChange.value: No change since 1980; it claims the small Matthew and Hunter islands, which France holds as part of New Caledonia.

alliancesRivals.value: Pacific Islands Forum; competition between China, Taiwan, Australia and the US for influence.

inventions.value: Traditional navigation by stars and swells.

scienceEducation.value: University of the South Pacific campuses.

openness.value: Open to trade and visitors, but dependent on imports of fuel, food and manufactured goods.

communicationTransport.value: Inter-island ships and small planes; the main airport is Bauerfield in Port Vila, and good roads exist mainly on Efate and Santo.

languageWriting.value: Bislama, English, French; over 100 local languages.

artsArchitecture.value: Tall carved slit-drums from Ambrym, sand drawings (on UNESCO’s heritage list) and the land diving (naghol) of Pentecost.

socialStructure.value: Village life is organised by kastom (custom), with chiefs and, in the north, graded societies in which men gain rank.

sharedIdentity.value: Pride in kastom, the Bislama language and independence, celebrated every year on 30 July.

dailyLife.value: Village houses of wood and thatch; meals of lap lap (a pudding of grated yam or taro), fish and island cabbage, with kava in the evening.

neighbours.value: New Caledonia (French) to the south-west, the Solomon Islands to the north-west and Fiji to the east.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity, Melanesian kastom beliefs, and Walter Lini’s “Melanesian socialism” in the 1980s.

colonisation.value: British–French condominium of the New Hebrides (1906–80).

riseSignals.value: The islands were first settled about 3,000 years ago, roughly between 1100 BCE and 700 BCE; Europeans first arrived in April 1606 (Queirós) and Cook named them the New Hebrides in 1774.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; tourism and seasonal work abroad grew strongly from the 2000s.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: France and the United Kingdom agreed in 1906 to rule the islands jointly; independence came on 30 July 1980.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
